source_evidence_candidates.before_quote:
Farhod’s narrative confirms that the choices prisoners make
that determine their caste position or status in prisoner society
are interwoven with their ethnic and religious identity, whether
this is self-ascribed or constructed for them. For the Uzbeks in
Farhod’s colony, placement in a ‘red barrack’ - that is, one for
the activist prisoners - was considered shameful and reflected
badly on the whole Uzbek community. As a result, substantial
efforts were made to dissuade newly arrived prisoners
from becoming activists, even though cooperating with the
administration could benefit them personally, such as in their
application for early release and access to enhanced privileges.
To counter the temptations to align with the administration,
Uzbek prisoners went out of their way to provide material support and mentoring to new arrivals; a member of the
Uzbek community would be assigned to visit fellow Uzbek
nationals fresh off the prison transport during their two-week
period of quarantine.
